source_title: Premium: The Hater's Guide To AI Debt (Part 1)
other_side: NLW treats the first cracks in data centre debt as a signal worth watching rather than a verdict. Jane Street-linked bonds have moved from 8.9% to 11.3%, Oracle-linked debt is quoted at 89 cents, and Meta's junk deal was heavily oversubscribed. Investors are still lending, he says, they just want more premium, and bond spreads are where to look if the AI trade turns. Zitron's Hater's Guide to AI Debt, published three days earlier (the free portion is summarised here; the rest is paywalled), argues the cracks are structural. In his telling Oracle, Google and Amazon have gone cash-flow negative, with Meta close behind, as capital spending eats almost every dollar the hyperscalers bring in. Neoclouds' revenues are 'a footnote' to their outgoings, and more than $500 billion of AI-related debt has already been raised in 2026 through bonds, special-purpose vehicles, convertibles and private credit, often from the same few lenders. And the need is growing just as money gets dearer: Goldman expects $400 billion of hyperscaler bonds in 2027, interest rates are rising for everyone, and NVIDIA has raised prices 15% on DRAM costs. His summary is that 'hundreds of billions of dollars are being invested to make single-digit billions of dollars maybe, some day'.
truth_beneath: Both men keep coming back to one question: can the AI build-out keep borrowing on terms it can afford? Both accept the facts. Debt, not cash, is now funding the data centres. Rates are rising. The weakest, junk-rated borrowers are paying much more. Anthropic's route to 'profitability' leaves out training costs and stock compensation. NLW's own guests warn that new data centre deals will add structural costs. The question that will settle it is whether the next round of data centre financing clears, and at what price. The thing to look for is spreads on new junk-rated and project-financed data centre deals over the coming quarter, plus whether Oracle keeps its investment-grade rating. What remains is worldview. NLW sees a normal credit market separating the haves from the have-nots while demand stays real. Zitron sees an industry that can only keep going by borrowing more, more expensively, against revenue that is not there. NLW is vindicated if investment-grade borrowers keep raising money comfortably and Anthropic's IPO prices well in November. Zitron is vindicated if a data centre deal fails to refinance or Oracle is downgraded. Both are polemicists with incentives, NLW bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is that both now point to the bond market, not share prices, as the place the truth will show first. Watch Oracle's credit rating.
